title: An Almost Entirely Unregulated Corner of the Health-Care Workforce
text:
When Mariah Stockman went into labor with her first child, her husband called their doula and told her to come to the hospital right away. Despite the urgency of the situation, the doula, Stockman said, asked her husband if she had time to stop and get a coffee. Two and a half hours later, the doula walked into Stockman’s delivery room. “I’ll never forget the coffee in her fucking hand,” Stockman told me recently.

 Her doula, she said, caught only the last 10 or so minutes of her labor, and she didn’t visit after the baby’s birth, as they had agreed on. Stockman said she paid $2,500 for the doula’s services: “What a waste.”

 Stockman is one of several women I interviewed who have had dissatisfying experiences with a birth doula, a role that makes up a fast-growing and largely unregulated part of the health-care workforce. (Stockman declined to share her doula’s name, because she believes that the woman is no longer working as a doula. I reached out to my other sources’ doulas and only two replied.) Doulas are meant to offer support and advocacy to women in labor. But some women I spoke with described doulas who missed appointments or even the birth of their baby, offered unsound medical advice, and otherwise behaved unprofessionally. And because doulas operate with minimal oversight, disappointed mothers tend to have little recourse.

 More and more people—mostly women—are both employing and becoming doulas. One recent meta-analysis found that doula support is associated with lower rates of C-sections—which are generally considered less optimal than vaginal births—and another concluded that women with doulas had “improved birth experiences.” The number of new doula health-care-provider registrations has increased 11 -fold since 2019, and doula services are now covered by Medicaid in 28 states, up from eight in 2022. At least eight states require coverage of doula services on commercial insurance plans. “More people know about doulas,” Erica Lane, the president of the doula-training-and-certifying body DONA International, told me. And for some mothers, “having a doula present at their birth drives them to become a doula.”

 [ Read: The states where it’s riskier to have a baby ] 

 Doula training varies considerably; a given doula might have a year of instruction or a couple of days’ worth. Doulas who pursue certification through DONA receive about 27 to 35 hours of training in topics such as childbirth and lactation, Lane said, and they must work with three families before receiving their credential. Or, a doula might have no training at all: Although some states require doulas to be certified in order to be reimbursed by Medicaid, there are no national standards for doula training or qualification.

 Social media—along with a keeping-up-with-the-Joneses’-baby mentality that takes hold in certain well-off women’s circles—can make some moms-to-be think that they simply must hire a birth doula. A well-designed Instagram post can portray a doula-attended birth as magical and goddessy. Lauren Salles Gumpert, a speech-language therapist and freelance writer in Virginia, told me that when she was pregnant, she read about other women’s “idyllic” labors and came away with the impression that “the doula is just kind of orchestrating the whole thing.” As she anticipated her own baby’s birth, she thought, “ I want this to be a beautiful day ” and “ if a doula can help make that happen, sure, I want that .”

 Gumpert’s experience with the doula she hired did not live up to this enchanting vision. A few weeks before her due date, Gumpert said her doula talked with her about “birth imprinting,” a debunked, pseudoscientific idea that the circumstances of a person’s birth permanently shape their nervous system. “I didn’t agree with everything that she said,” Gumpert said, although at that point she still felt good about the doula overall. Other women I spoke with also said that their doulas dispensed questionable counsel; one mother in Seattle told me that her doula had encouraged her to decline pitocin, a medication that can induce contractions, against medical advice.

 The most common complaint I encountered concerned doulas not showing up for all or part of the birth, or behaving in strange, unsupportive ways once they did get there. Gumpert’s doula left her hospital room while she was in labor to go see another client, which made Gumpert feel as though the doula was “abandoning me and completely disregarding my experience.” When the doula eventually texted to check in, Gumpert told her not to return. (Gumpert’s doula, Leslie Cuffee, told me that her recollection “differs from the account presented” and that she is “committed to providing compassionate, individualized care, support, and availability to every family I serve.”) Jessica Braga, a mother in Grand Rapids, Michigan, said that her doula missed three appointments with Braga over the course of four months—once because she was at the grocery store, and another time, she told Braga, because her “computer was fried.” When Braga was seven and a half months pregnant, she hired a new doula, with whom she had a positive experience, she said.

 Emily Morgan, a mother in Oklahoma, told me she hired a doula for her first birth because she’d had minimal experience with babies or childbirth. Her doula arrived hours after Morgan was admitted to the hospital in labor, she said, and when she did appear, she brought along her own 3-year-old daughter—who lifted Morgan’s hospital gown and touched her belly. Morgan said that the doula dipped in and out of the hospital room throughout her two-day stay without telling her why she was leaving or where she was going, and that as Morgan pushed her baby out, the doula discussed hospital drama with a nurse. “They were just in their own world, chatting,” Morgan said.

 [ Read: A long-standing theory of childbirth is a myth ] 

 Morgan’s doula offered a partial refund if she agreed not to speak negatively about her, but Morgan declined. Other mothers told me they did ask their doulas for refunds but had trouble collecting. Although some organizations, including DONA, have grievance procedures for misconduct, no central oversight body evaluates complaints against doulas. In a recent case in Maryland, the state attorney general’s consumer-protection division issued an order against the operators of a doula company that had billed customers tens of thousands of dollars and failed to provide the paid-for care or to issue refunds. “Many consumers, they just did not get services at all,” Lauren Bell, an assistant attorney general, told me. “Meaning, just total not showing up for labor and delivery.”

 One Albuquerque mother, who asked not to be identified because she is still negotiating with her former doula, said that on the morning of her scheduled induction, which her doula was contracted to be present for, her doula texted her “Good luck today!” She then went dark and arrived at the hospital more than two hours later, when the mother had already been taken to the operating room for an emergency C-section. The doula met with the mother about 40 minutes after the surgery. “She just sat down and was playing on her cellphone,” the mother said, and then promptly left to go see another client. When I spoke with the mother, she said the doula was still refusing to issue her a full refund. (According to texts I reviewed, the doula thought that the mother would send her additional texts during the induction process and didn’t want to bother her.)

 [ Read: A striking decline in openness to IVF ] 

 These mothers’ experiences don’t mean that all doulas are negligent or unnecessary; many people report that their doula was helpful. Some of the women I interviewed who had disappointing doulas went on to hire a different doula and were pleased with their services. Lindsay Mallick, a maternal-health researcher who has studied doulas, told me that “having that emotional support can increase oxytocin,” a hormone that can speed up contractions and help the mother feel good during labor. Black women, who have higher rates of maternal mortality and report sometimes feeling ignored by the medical system, have told researchers that they find the presence of a doula especially beneficial . Still, the field would benefit from better standards. “There should be some regulation,” Kathleen Hoke, a professor of public-health law at the University of Maryland, told me, “whether that’s based on receiving a certification or having a certain level of experience that you can attest to and have others attest to.”

 In the meantime, the mothers and researchers I spoke with recommended choosing an experienced, certified doula who has a substitute available around the due date. “It is very irresponsible to sign a client without a solid backup in place,” Lane, from DONA, said. Another option is to consider whether a family member or friend can provide the kind of emotional support a doula offers: Evidence suggests that untrained labor companions can be just as useful as formal doulas. Some of the women I spoke with were so scarred by their experience that they would now consider only a doula they already knew personally, who would help them for free. With a professional doula, “I don’t think the relationship can be sincere, because they are getting paid,” Gumpert told me. “At the end of the day, it’s all a business.” For her, true support during labor wasn’t something money could buy.
